The White grunt, Haemulon plumierii, requires detailed life-history data collected from field populations throughout its Caribbean and western Atlantic range. Recent surveys in the Gulf of Mexico have documented the maximum size attainable by this commercially important grunt, with the largest individuals reaching a total length of 53 centimeters [Li = 53 centimeters]. This ultimate length places the species among the larger members of the genus Haemulon, though individuals of this size are relatively uncommon and likely represent older, slow-growing adults that have avoided fishing mortality. The neonatal stage begins with the release of fertilised eggs into the water column, where the newly emerged yolk-sac larvae carry an extremely modest initial wet weight of 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], a value derived from estimated egg dimensions that reflect the planktotrophic larval strategy typical of this family.

The transition from the pelagic larval phase to a demersal, reef-associated juvenile marks a critical period of habitat shift for Haemulon plumierii. During their first year of life, post-settlement juveniles grow rapidly as they exploit the structural complexity of seagrass beds and coral rubble for shelter and foraging opportunities. At the onset of sexual maturation, individuals reach a total length at puberty of 18.3 centimeters [Lp = 18.3 centimeters], a size that typically corresponds to an age of roughly one to two years depending on local environmental conditions. This length threshold at puberty represents the point at which gametogenesis begins and the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis becomes fully activated, marking the individual as a reproductively viable sub-adult. Achieving this size is an important demographic milestone, as it allows the fish to transition from a strictly somatic growth phase to one that includes allocation of resources toward gonad development and eventual spawning activity.

Once Haemulon plumierii reaches its adult size, the maximum recorded wet weight attained by the largest sexually mature individuals has been documented at 4,400 grams [Wwi = 4,400 grams]. This asymptotic mass corresponds closely to the ultimate length of 53 centimeters and is typically observed only in older, slow-growing females that have accumulated considerable somatic tissue over many years. The species exhibits a characteristic growth pattern common among lutjanid and haemulid fishes, where mass increases rapidly in the juvenile and early adult stages before decelerating markedly near the asymptotic size. This ultimate wet weight provides a useful benchmark for fisheries stock assessments and for constructing size-based yield-per-recruit models, as it defines the upper boundary of somatic growth potential under natural conditions. Age estimates derived from otolith increment counts indicate that the species' maximum lifespan in the wild reaches approximately 8,030 days [am = approximately 8,030 days] at a mean annual water temperature of 25.9 degrees Celsius [T = 25.9 degrees Celsius].

Reproductive output in the White grunt varies substantially across its geographic range, but recent studies conducted in the Florida Keys have characterized its maximum potential fecundity under optimal thermal conditions. At a sustained water temperature of 25.9 degrees Celsius [T = 25.9 degrees Celsius], an individual female can produce an estimated 855 eggs per day [Ri = 855 eggs per day] during the peak spawning season. This daily reproductive rate reflects the species' iteroparous, batch-spawning strategy, wherein females release multiple clutches of pelagic eggs over an extended spawning period that spans from spring through early autumn. The observed maximum of 855 eggs per day is the product of a moderate clutch size combined with a high spawning frequency, a pattern that allows the species to distribute reproductive effort across the entire warm season and buffer against stochastic mortality events affecting any single batch. Temperature plays a crucial role in regulating vitellogenesis and oocyte development, which explains the tight coupling between the 25.9 degrees Celsius thermal regime and the peak fecundity estimates.

Comparative physiological studies within the family Haemulidae offer additional context for interpreting the life-history strategy of Haemulon plumierii. Related species such as the bluestriped grunt (Haemulon sciurus) and the French grunt (Haemulon flavolineatum) exhibit similar body plans but typically achieve smaller maximum lengths and shorter lifespans. The White grunt's maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 8,030 days [am = approximately 8,030 days] under natural thermal conditions at 25.9 degrees Celsius [T = 25.9 degrees Celsius] is notably extended, even among congeners, suggesting a relatively slower pace of life that may be linked to its larger ultimate body size. This longevity allows individuals to accumulate multiple years of reproductive experience, thereby compensating for the relatively modest daily egg production of 855 eggs per day [Ri = 855 eggs per day] through repeated spawning events across many seasons. Future research should focus on quantifying whether individuals at the northern edge of the species' range experience reduced growth rates and shortened lifespans due to cooler thermal regimes, and how such variation might alter the population's resilience to fishing pressure.
